questions.question: Which Python expression is the direct counterpart of ∀x P(x) over a finite domain?
questions.explanation: all() checks every element; any() is the existential. Python already speaks quantifier.

questions.question: A predicate is…
options: a sentence that is definitely true
a proposition with variable holes that becomes true/false once filled
questions.explanation: P(x) = "x is prime" is neither true nor false until x is fixed — then it becomes a proposition.

questions.question: "Not everyone passed the exam" is equivalent to…
options: someone did not pass the exam
questions.explanation: Negating a universal gives an existential with a negated predicate — the flip rule this lesson formalizes.

questions.question: An existential claim ∃x P(x) is established by…
options: exhibiting one witness where P holds
assuming P and finding a contradiction
questions.explanation: One concrete example settles an ∃; that element is called the witness.

questions.question: Over the empty domain, ∀x P(x) is…
options: true, vacuously — no x can fail it
true only if P is the empty predicate
questions.explanation: A universal over no elements is a kept promise about nothing; the lesson script checks this case explicitly.

questions.question: The negation of ∀x P(x) is…
questions.explanation: Denying "all" requires only one counterexample: some x failing P. The quantifier flips, the predicate negates.

questions.question: The negation of ∃x P(x) is…
questions.explanation: Ruling out "some" means P fails for every element — all-not. SQL's NOT EXISTS is this rule in practice.

questions.question: ∀x ∃y (y < x) versus ∃y ∀x (y < x) over the integers: which is true?
options: Only the first — each x has some smaller y; no single y sits below all x
questions.explanation: Quantifier order is meaning: per-element helpers vs one helper serving everyone. The lesson code demonstrates both verdicts.

questions.question: Why can ∀x ∃y (y < x) be true over all integers yet false on a finite slice like [-3, 3]?
options: Because finite slices use different math
Because the smallest element of the slice has nothing below it — a boundary failure
Because the slice is too small to compute
It cannot — the claim has the same truth value on both
questions.explanation: A claim true over an infinite domain can fail at the boundary of a finite one. Always probe the edges.

questions.question: In the proof that ¬∀x P(x) ⇒ ∃x ¬P(x), the key move is…
options: suppose no x fails P; then all satisfy P — contradicting ¬∀x P(x)
proving P holds for a witness
questions.explanation: Contradiction: ruling out the negation of the target forces the target. This is Phase 01's technique arriving early.

questions.question: "Users with no orders" in SQL is best expressed using…
options: NOT EXISTS — the ∀x ¬P(x) form, which indexes correctly
questions.explanation: "No orders" is ¬∃ order. The negation table turns it into NOT EXISTS — the form the query planner can use.
